segments.text: Five words — and the same point vaṇakkam made, told again in numbers: Tamil counts with its own words, not borrowed ones.

blocks.title: You'll want to know: The five

segments.text: There is a table here I cannot read to you — 4 columns and 5 rows, and it has more columns than can be held in the ear at once. Its columns are: one with no heading, numeral, word, said. Come back and look at it when you have stopped.

Two writing systems sit side by side here: the word (spelled out in letters) and the numeral (a single symbol — ௧ ௨ ௩ ௪ ௫, Tamil's own digits, as distinct from 1 2 3 4 5 as they are from Roman I II III). You'll meet the digits again whenever a price or a page number is written in Tamil.

If you're doing the writing track, you can already read pieces of these: ந and ன (the n-family), ற the hard r inside mūṉṟu, and the puḷḷi dot that stacks ன்ற into the single cluster you hear in ஒன்று and மூன்று.

Count to five in Tamil. (Oṉṟu, iraṇṭu, mūṉṟu, nāṉku, aintu.) Are Tamil's numbers borrowed from Sanskrit, like Hindi's? (No — they're native Dravidian.) Which two writing systems sit side by side? (Spelled-out words and Tamil's own numerals.) Next: compare these native forms across the family.

segments.text: Hindi's number forms are Sanskrit worn smooth. Tamil's are native Dravidian, so their sister-language shapes reveal the family directly.

blocks.title: The word, taken apart - The cousin table

segments.text: There is a table here I cannot read to you — 5 columns and 4 rows, and it has more columns than can be held in the ear at once. Its columns are: one with no heading, Tamil, Kannada, Telugu, Malayalam. Come back and look at it when you have stopped.
Each row is one word in four regional coats. That shared skeleton is why one Dravidian language gives you a running start on another.
One is less tidy: Tamil oṉṟu, Kannada ondu, and Malayalam onnu share old oṉ-, while Telugu uses the separate formation okaṭi. The family agrees more neatly on 2–5 than on 1.

blocks.title: Sounds you'll need: Hear the Tamil cluster

segments.text: In oṉṟu and mūṉṟu, ன்ற is alveolar n running into hard ṟ, almost one knock: on-ru, muun-ru. Puḷḷi on ன் removes its vowel before the cluster.

segments.instruction: oṉṟu and mūṉṟu, holding ன்ற together

segments.text: Are these forms borrowed? (No, native Dravidian.) Which numbers stay tidiest across the family? (Two through five.) Which language forms "one" differently? (Telugu, okaṭi.)

blocks.title: You'll want to know: Seven carries the letter that names the language

segments.text: Look at ஏழு (ēḻu, seven). Its middle letter is ழ — the retroflex approximant, the sound English can only clumsily spell zh. It is the rarest and most characteristic sound in Tamil, and it sits inside the language's own name: Tamiḻ (தமிழ்) ends in this very letter. So seven is a free daily rehearsal of the sound that says who the language is. Curl the tongue back, don't touch, and voice it: ē-ḻu.
(You met its cousin ற — the hard ṟ — back in ஆறு / āṟu, six. Tamil keeps these apart carefully: ஆறு āṟu and ஏழு ēḻu end in two different sounds English would both call "r/zh".)

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: Nine is built from words you already have

segments.text: ஒன்பது (oṉpatu, nine) is not a fresh word to memorise — it is two you already know, joined:
ஒன் (oṉ-, "one," from last lesson) + பது (patu, "ten") becomes ஒன்பது = "one‑to‑ten" — one short of ten.
And ten itself is பத்து (pattu). Say oṉpatu then pattu and you can hear nine leaning on ten. That is a common Dravidian habit — nine described as one-away-from-ten rather than named outright.

segments.text: Count six to ten in Tamil. (Āṟu, ēḻu, eṭṭu, oṉpatu, pattu.) Which number is written with ழ, and where else does that letter appear? (Seven, ēḻu — the same letter that ends Tamiḻ.) How is nine built? (Oṉ "one" + patu "ten" becomes oṉpatu, one short of ten.) Next: the puḷḷi — the dot that takes a consonant's built-in vowel away.

segments.text: Every consonant carries a built-in a. So how do you write a consonant with no vowel — the k in vaṇakkam, or the m at the end?
One dot.
க = ka becomes க் = k.
புள்ளி (puḷḷi) means simply "the dot." Written above a letter, it removes the inherent vowel. That's the whole rule.

A standing note for this whole track. These lessons quote real Tamil words and examples, and most of them contain letters the track has not taught you to draw yet — puḷḷi's own name uses ப, ள and the ு sign, and the comparisons below reach for others again. Read anything printed here; only draw the letters a lesson has actually broken into strokes. The data file behind this track covers 11 letters so far and says so (complete: false) — it grows as the chapters need it.

blocks.title: Script you'll notice: What Tamil does not do

segments.text: If you have done the Devanagari track, this is the moment to notice a real divergence.

In Devanagari, killing the vowel makes the bare consonant fuse with the next one into a squeezed conjunct — स् + त becomes स्त, and the first letter loses its spine. The virama usually disappears into the ligature.
Tamil doesn't do that. The dot stays visible, and both letters keep their full shape:

utterances: Devanagari, स् + त becomes स्त — a new fused shape.
Tamil, க் + க becomes க்க — two letters, dot intact.

segments.text: The consequence is arithmetic. Tamil's whole set is 247 characters: 12 vowels + 18 consonants + the 216 consonant-vowel combinations + the āytam ஃ. That is genuinely all of them. Devanagari's conjuncts run to many hundreds of ligature shapes on top of its letters, each to be learned or at least recognised.
(One honest exception: Tamil does have a few ligatures borrowed with Sanskrit words — க்ஷ kṣa and ஸ்ரீ śrī. They sit outside the 18 native consonants and outside the 247.)

segments.source: [YOU WRITE: க் — "க, then the dot above"]

segments.instruction: க்க — two full letters, dot intact, no fusing
segments.source: [YOU WRITE: க்க — two full letters, dot intact, **no fusing**]

segments.text: What does the puḷḷi do, and what does the word mean? (Removes the inherent vowel; puḷḷi is simply "the dot".) What does Devanagari do that Tamil doesn't? (Fuses the letters into a conjunct — Tamil keeps both shapes and the dot.) What does Tamil get in exchange? (A much smaller character set — 247, with almost no ligatures: only the borrowed க்ஷ and ஸ்ரீ.) Next: six, seven and ten across the family.

lessons.title: Six to ten — family resemblances and one Kannada shift
lessons.gloss: six, seven, and ten stay family cousins while Kannada regularly softens p to h

segments.text: The Tamil forms are learned. Now use their sister shapes as evidence for inheritance and regular sound change.

blocks.title: The word, taken apart - The stable cousins

segments.text: Six and seven remain close: Tamil āṟu, Kannada āru, Malayalam āṟu; Tamil ēḻu, Kannada ēḷu, Malayalam ēḻu. Tamil and Malayalam also keep eight and nine nearly identical: eṭṭu and oṉpatu/onpatu.
Telugu wanders on eight and nine with enimidi and tommidi, so those forms are less reliable as family-wide recognition anchors.

blocks.title: The word, taken apart - pattu becomes hattu

segments.text: Tamil and Malayalam say pattu, while Kannada says hattu. The initial p becomes h is a regular Kannada shift, not a random replacement. Compare Tamil pāl, "milk," with Kannada hālu.
A correspondence lets differences prove relationship: repeated p/h pairs are stronger evidence than one accidental resemblance.

segments.text: What happens to Tamil pattu in Kannada? (P regularly softens to h: hattu.) Which second pair confirms the pattern? (Pāl / hālu, "milk.") Which language diverges most on eight and nine? (Telugu.)
